add_nodes.title: First water mined from lunar polar ice
add_nodes.description: A pilot plant digs ice-bearing regolith in or beside a permanently shadowed crater at the lunar south pole and extracts at least 1 t of water in one campaign, measured and stored. It is the step between the first ice measurements and a lunar propellant supply.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No ice extraction has been tried on the Moon. The form of polar ice is unknown: in lab tests excavation energy for ice-cemented simulant rises 52x as ice goes from 1 to 12 wt%, while pressure-sintered simulant gets easier to dig (Space and Planetary Resources, Sep 2026). NASA's IPEx is designed to dig about 20 t of regolith per mission. Ground truth from PROSPECT (2027), VIPER, LUPEX or Chang'e-8 is expected in 2027-29. Permanently shadowed regions sit near 40 K, so power must come by cable from a sunlit rim or from a reactor.
add_nodes.why: At 5 wt% ice, 1 t of water means digging and heating about 20 t of regolith, the scale IPEx was built for (general arithmetic). AI enters through the validated regolith model and model-based excavator design, which size the machine to the ice form found in 2028-29. Once a pilot runs, extraction takes days to weeks, so water comes in the landing year. Chain (S2): ground truth 2028 -> regolith model 2029 and excavator design 2030 -> pilot funded, built and qualified 2030-32 -> landed on a heavy cargo flight and 1 t extracted 2033. S3: model and design a year earlier and cadence 0.5-1 year faster -> 2032. S1: excavator design in 2032 plus the same three-year build-and-land lag -> 2035. The reactor option lands in 2033 at the earliest, so the pilot depends on a cable from a sunlit rim. No extraction payload is funded, and NASA ISRU payloads have taken about five years from selection to flight (PRIME-1, general). Power in the polar dark, funding and landing success remain, so S3 and S4 are Medium by 2035 and S1 and S2 are Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Early bases may skip ice and make oxygen from sunlit regolith, which needs no cold-trap operations. If the ice is vapor-deposited and hard, or patchy, a pilot may extract far less than 1 t per campaign.
add_nodes.signpost: NASA, SpaceX, Blue Origin or CNSA manifests an ice-extraction payload with a stated water target on a 2030-33 lander; a polar dataset fixes the ice form.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: ice data from 2028-29 and routine heavy cargo put a first water pilot inside the 2035 horizon. S2 is Low because no extraction payload is funded and one would need funding by about 2030. S4 equals S3 because power in permanently shadowed craters and funding bind, and few general-purpose robots will work at 40 K by 2035.

add_nodes.title: Lunar oxygen fuels landers at 10 t a year
add_nodes.description: A second-generation lunar plant makes oxygen at an annualized 10 t a year or more, from regolith or from polar ice, and at least 1 t of it is liquefied and transferred into a lander or depot as propellant. Oxygen is about 78% of methalox propellant mass, so this is the first step toward lunar-made propellant.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No lunar plant exists. A 2025 systems study sizes a 10 t/yr molten regolith electrolysis plant at about 1.1 kg/h and under 30 kW. The best ground run made 0.07 kg/h for 9 h (the KSC and Lunar Resources LR-1 rig, late 2024). A Starship return would need about 65 kg/h of oxygen. NASA's Lunar Reactor-1 (100 kWe) targets launch readiness in late 2029, and the model dates a 100 kWe reactor on the Moon to 2033 (struct-fsp-lunar-100kwe).
add_nodes.why: A 10 t/yr plant runs about 8,800 h a year at 1.1 kg/h, so anode life, a feed of tens of tonnes of regolith a year and power through the lunar night set the pace. It follows the 1 t/yr pilot by 2-3 years: one cycle to learn from pilot data and land a larger unit. AI reactor models and anode discovery shorten the design half of that cycle. Chain (S3): pilot 2031 -> second unit designed 2032 -> landed and at rate 2034. S2: pilot 2032 -> 2035. S1: pilot 2034 -> beyond 2035. S4 equals S3. The plant is designed, built and qualified on Earth, where robots reach suppliers after 2031 and each new process needs 6-24 months of requalification. On the Moon one excavator covers the regolith feed. Landing, funding and a buyer bind, so S2-S4 are Low by 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: No buyer needs lunar oxygen while Starship brings oxygen from Earth at falling cost. A plant at this scale may run as a demonstration, and liquefaction and storage add power and mass that a pilot never tested.
add_nodes.signpost: A funded second-generation ISRU plant with a 10 t/yr target and a named delivery date; a lunar pilot that runs more than 3,000 h in a year.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: the lunar oxygen spine reaches propellant scale inside the horizon in S2-S4, first in 2034 in S3 and S4, and is Low by 2035. S4 equals S3 because plant build, anode life, power and a buyer bind.

add_nodes.title: A hundred robots work on the Moon at once
add_nodes.description: At least 100 robots of 20 kg or more (rovers, excavators, manipulators or humanoid-class machines) do excavation, hauling, construction or maintenance on the lunar surface at the same time, survive the lunar night, and are supervised by a ground team of fewer than 50 people using AI planning and machine-checked plans.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Fewer than ten robots have ever worked on the Moon at once (general), and most lasted one lunar day. CADRE (late 2026) will test a three-rover team. NASA's Moon Base plan foresees up to 30 CLPS landings from 2027, and NASA moved to raise the CLPS contract ceiling to $4.2B in May 2026 (SpaceNews via 33FG). Perseverance flew its first AI-planned drives in Dec 2025.
add_nodes.why: Two curves meet here. AI planning with machine-checked plans cuts operator time per robot severalfold by 2029 (S2), and 100 robots of 20-100 kg weigh 2-10 t, a fraction of one heavy cargo landing. What remains is the supply of lunar-rated robots, night survival and base power. Chain (S3): heavy cargo 2028 and ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2 (2030) -> robots from several programs accumulate -> 100 at once in 2032. S2: 2033. S1: 2035. In S1-S3 lunar robots stay bespoke and programs fly a few per landing, so S2 and S3 are Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative. S4 keeps the S3 year, because robots landing before 2032 fly on hardware frozen in 2027-28. By 2035 S4 rises to Medium: robot variants of Earth designs reach lunar hardware after 2031, and the S4 robot path puts hundreds of robots off Earth by 2035 if cargo reaches ten landings a year. Lunar units still need new actuators, lubricants, seals, thermal control and electronics for vacuum, dust and about -170 to +120 C, so S4 stays below High.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Lunar robots stay bespoke, short-lived and expensive. Programs may fly a few large machines instead of many small ones, and the count says little about useful work.
add_nodes.signpost: A Moon Base or commercial operator reports 25 or more robots active at once through a lunar night; a humanoid-class robot flown to the Moon.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: the productivity chain reaches fleet scale inside the horizon. S4 keeps the S3 year (2032) and rises from Low to Medium by 2035, because the count of lunar-rated robots binds and robot variants of Earth designs supply it after 2031. Landed mass and night power keep S4 below High.

Description now requires robots of 20 kg or more doing real work. auton-moon-base-infrastructure moved from soft to hard (night survival for 100 robots needs base power). The S4 analysis puts off-Earth general-purpose robots at tens in 2031 and hundreds by 2035 on the S4 base path, and only with ten cargo landings a year. S1-S3 run the slower robot path and robo-lunar-construction is Low in S3, so bespoke fleets in S1-S3 rarely reach 100. Binding gate stays fabrication: the metric is the robot count, and landed mass for 100 robots is a fraction of one landing. add_nodes.title: Crews stay on the Moon for 90 days or more
add_nodes.description: A crew of two or more lives at a lunar surface base for 90 days or longer in one stay, and the base runs itself between crews. It marks the start of long-duration presence (Moon Base Phase 3).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: The longest lunar surface stay is about 75 hours (Apollo 17, 1972; general). Artemis II flew in Apr 2026, and the first Artemis landing is planned for 2028, with crewed landings about every six months at first. Reporting dates Moon Base Phase 3, long-duration presence, to 2032 onward. NASA was reported near bulk launch buys for its roughly $30B Moon Base (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6 2026). China plans a crewed landing by 2030 and a research station in the 2030s (general).
add_nodes.why: A 90-day stay needs a pressurized habitat with power through three lunar nights, life support with spares, local medical and fault response, and a rescue option. It also needs a ride home that waits 90 days on the surface with its propellant kept cold, or a second crewed vehicle. AI contributes through crew-side diagnosis, sparing models and a base that maintains itself between stays. Chain (S2): Phase 2 elements and crew-optional operations 2031 -> a pressurized habitat and night power in place 2032-33 -> first 90-day stay 2033. S3: 2032. S1: 2035. Appropriations, human rating and landing safety do not compress, and both hard parents are Medium by 2035, so S2-S4 are Low and S1 is Speculative.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Government flagships slip 2-7 years. A budget fight, a landing accident or a radiation policy can hold stays to weeks until well past 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: NASA or a partner contracts a surface habitat with a named 2031-33 delivery; a crew stays more than 30 days on the Moon.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: Moon Base Phase 3 puts long stays inside the 2035 horizon, but a pressurized habitat, night power and a ride home must all arrive in time, so S2-S4 are Low. S4 equals S3 because appropriations, human rating and landing safety bind.

S4 = S3 (institution- and appropriations-bound). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): band_2035 S1 Low -> Speculative and S2-S4 Medium -> Low (skeptic). The stay needs both Medium hard parents, a habitat beyond Phase 2's semi-habitable element, night power with fission Low by 2035, and a ride home; Artemis-era stays are planned at about a week. Soft inputs from prop-cfm-models (cold ascent propellant) and the cargo-cadence node. The advocate's soft edge from robo-lunar-construction is not added: it lands later than this node in every scenario.

add_nodes.title: Crops grown through repeated harvests on the Moon
add_nodes.description: A pressurized plant module at a lunar base completes at least three successive harvests of a food crop under model-based stability control, tended by crew or robots. It is the first bioregenerative food and air step beyond seed sprouting.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Chang'e-4 sprouted a cotton seed on the Moon in 2019, and it died within days (general). NASA's LEAF plant experiment is planned for an early Artemis landing (general). China's Lunar Palace 1 ran a 370-day crewed closed test on the ground in 2017-18. MELiSSA is working toward full loop closure in its pilot plant (ICES 2025).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); family 149 enters only through the conditional stability-theory accelerator
add_nodes.why: Crop cycles of 60-120 days make three harvests take 6-12 months, and lighting a module through 14-day nights takes hundreds of watts per square meter of growing area (general). A ground-validated controlled loop comes first. Chain (S3): closed ground test 2030 and ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2 (2030) -> module landed 2032 -> three harvests 2033. S2: 2034. S1: its ground test lands in 2034, so beyond 2035. Funding and biology set the clock, so every scenario is Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Physico-chemical life support and food shipped from Earth stay cheaper at base scale through 2035, so plant modules remain small experiments.
add_nodes.signpost: A lunar greenhouse payload with a multi-harvest goal on a Moon Base or Chinese research-station manifest.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: it extends the bioregenerative chain from ground tests to the Moon inside the horizon. S4 equals S3 because crop cycles and funding bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edges from auton-blss-closed-test and auton-moon-base-infrastructure; soft from stability theory, long crew stays and fission power. S4 = S3 (biology clock and funding). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): Text only: base power is ridge solar from Moon Base Phase 2, since the 100 kWe reactor is 2033 in every scenario (advocate).

add_nodes.title: Robots prepare a Mars landing site and power
add_nodes.description: Robots delivered by a 20 t-class Mars landing deploy at least 100 kW of power, survey and dig for ice, and prepare a site for later ships, working through at least one Mars season under Earth supervision with a one-way light time of 3-22 minutes.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No robot has deployed power or prepared a site on Mars. SpaceX put Mars work on hold in Feb 2026 to prioritize the Moon and skipped the late-2026 window. Windows inside the horizon: Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031 and about Apr 2033, with landings in late 2029, late 2031 and late 2033. A Starship-scale propellant plant needs megawatt-class power.
add_nodes.why: Lunar robot operations train the methods, and AI planning with machine-checked plans lets a small team supervise across the light-time delay. Mars adds a 26-month gap between deliveries. Chain (S2 and S3): a 20 t-class landing in late 2031 carries robots and arrays -> 100 kW deployed and a site surveyed during 2032. S1: weaker autonomy and the 2033 window -> 2034. Each window allows one try and a new vehicle class lands well below certainty, so S2-S4 are Low by 2035 and S1 is Speculative.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may use the 2031 and 2033 windows for landing tests only and send no working robots, and power hardware that survives Mars dust storms may not be ready.
add_nodes.signpost: A Mars cargo manifest for the 2031 or 2033 window that lists robots and surface power.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: the late-2031 and late-2033 Mars landings fall inside the horizon, and a propellant plant needs robots to set up power first. S4 equals S3 because Mars windows bind, and general-purpose robots add no windows.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-moon-mars (2035 horizon, S4): added. Hard edge from hyper-mars-heavy-landing and hard edge into auton-mars-propellant-plant (a plant cannot run before robots deploy its power); soft from the lunar robot fleet, surface productivity, verified autonomy, excavation design and the Mars ISRU demo. S4 = S3 (launch windows). | R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): Soft edge from robo-lunar-construction removed (skeptic): it lands later than this node in every scenario and crosses to another planet. Years and bands unchanged.

add_nodes.title: Ten heavy cargo landings on the Moon in one year
add_nodes.description: Ten or more cargo landings of at least 10 t each reach the lunar surface in one calendar year, from Starship, Blue Moon or other heavy landers. It is the landed-mass rate behind lunar outpost work after 2031.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No heavy cargo has landed on the Moon. Starship reached orbit on Sep 28, 2026, and ship-to-ship propellant transfer is expected in early 2027. In Feb 2026 SpaceX made a lunar city its priority. NASA's Moon Base plan (Mar 2026) foresees up to 30 CLPS landings, NASA moved to raise the CLPS ceiling to $4.2B (May 2026, SpaceNews via 33FG), and it was reported near bulk launch buys for the roughly $30B Moon Base (Bloomberg via 33FG, Oct 6, 2026).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: This node is an exogenous anchor with no AI-math pathway. Each Starship lunar cargo landing needs on the order of ten tanker launches or more (public estimates vary; general), so ten landings need 100 or more heavy launches in a year. The launch clock passes 100 heavy launches a year about 2030 (S3 2029) and reaches hundreds by the mid-2030s, so demand and lander production decide. Chain (S3): first heavy cargo 2028 -> two to four a year in 2030-31 -> ten in 2032. S2: 2033. S1: 2034. The budgets of one or two customers and landing failures keep S2-S4 at Medium by 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: NASA's budget buys only a few heavy landings a year, and SpaceX may hold its own lunar flights until propellant transfer and landing are routine. One landing failure can pause a fleet for months.
add_nodes.signpost: A contract or company plan for five or more heavy lunar cargo landings in one year; two heavy cargo landings within six months.
add_nodes.note_2035: New node: it makes explicit the landed-mass rate behind the 2033-35 lunar outcomes and the S4 analysis's off-Earth robot count. S4 equals S3 because launch binds and robots add at most about 1.4x to launch campaigns.
add_nodes.revision_note: R-moon-mars resolver (2026-10-07): added from the acceleration advocate. Both reviewers found that the 10+ cargo landings a year behind the reviewed lunar S4 credits had no node. Hard edges from auton-lunar-heavy-cargo-landing and physclock-heavy-cadence-100; soft from the refueling economy, cheap internal launch cost and robot launch refurbishment (robo-earth-pads-plants dropped: S4 2035 is after this node). Soft edges out to the 10 t/yr oxygen plant, the robot fleet, long stays and robo-lunar-construction. No S4 credit.

patch.thesis: AI-planned, machine-checked operations give lunar and Mars robots severalfold more work per operator by about 2029 (base case). A self-running Moon base and tonne-scale lunar oxygen are Medium by 2035. Landed mass, night power, funding and Mars windows set the pace. S4 robots add one band only to the size of the lunar robot fleet.
